title: Telnet Protocol Specification
subtitle: The original remote-terminal protocol: one TCP connection, an imaginary standard terminal, and a polite way to negotiate extras.
summary: Telnet carries a terminal session between two hosts over a single TCP connection on port 23. To avoid every host needing to know every other host's terminal quirks, both ends pretend to be a Network Virtual Terminal (NVT), a plain seven-bit ASCII device. Optional extras are agreed with a four-word negotiation (WILL, WON'T, DO, DON'T), and special commands travel in-band behind a one-byte escape, IAC (255). Telnet sends everything unencrypted, so SSH has replaced it for logging in.

eli5.summary: Telnet is like a very long phone cord for your keyboard and screen. Both computers first agree to act like the same simple, boring screen, and then they can ask each other politely, "Can we do something fancier?" and the other one can say yes or no.

questions: what is a network virtual terminal
why was telnet replaced by ssh

tldr.problem: Every host had its own kind of terminal and its own way of doing things like interrupting a runaway program, so remote logins between different systems were a mess.
tldr.mechanism: Both ends act as a Network Virtual Terminal over one TCP connection (server port 23). Control functions and option negotiation are sent in the data stream as byte sequences starting with IAC (255).
tldr.outcome: Telnet is an Internet Standard (STD 8) and its NVT and option model still underlie many terminal-style protocols, but because it has no encryption it has been replaced by SSH for remote login.

today: Telnet is rarely used to log in to servers any more, because everything it sends, including passwords, crosses the network in the clear; SSH (RFC 4253) took over that job. The protocol itself is still used to talk to routers, switches and embedded devices on trusted management networks, and command-line telnet clients are still used to test whether a TCP port accepts connections. Its option model lives on in the many Telnet options that followed RFC 855, and RFC 1123 later added host requirements for Telnet implementations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The purpose of Telnet, in the RFC's words, is "to provide a fairly general, bi-directional, eight-bit byte oriented communications facility." Its main goal is a standard method of connecting terminal devices and terminal-oriented processes to each other. The authors also expect it could link two terminals ("linking") or two processes (distributed computation).

A Telnet connection is simply a TCP connection (RFC 793) that carries data with Telnet control information mixed in. The protocol rests on three ideas: a Network Virtual Terminal, negotiated options, and a symmetric view of terminals and processes. The RFC is short, 15 pages, and replaces the earlier specification in RFC 764.

The "user" host is the one the physical terminal is attached to, and the "server" host is the one providing a service. Alternatively, the user host is simply whichever host started the communication.
sections.eli5: Telnet lets your keyboard and screen talk to another computer through the network, as if a very long cable ran between them.

sections.title: The Network Virtual Terminal
sections.content:
When a connection opens, each end is assumed to be a Network Virtual Terminal (NVT), "an imaginary device which provides a standard, network-wide, intermediate representation of a canonical terminal." Each host maps its own real devices onto the NVT, so neither side needs to know anything about the other's terminals. That is the key trade: each host needs only one mapping, to the NVT, rather than a mapping for every other kind of terminal.

The NVT has a printer and a keyboard. The printer shows incoming data; the keyboard produces outgoing data. The code set is seven-bit USASCII carried in an eight-bit field. By default the NVT is treated as a half-duplex, line-buffered device even though the underlying TCP connection is full duplex: data is gathered locally until a complete line is ready or a local signal says to send. Implementers are told to provide a way to flush buffered data immediately.

Printer codes
Only NUL (0), LF (10) and CR (13) must have an effect. BEL (7), BS (8), HT (9), VT (11) and FF (12) have defined but optional effects.
Keyboard
Can generate all 128 USASCII codes, plus the extra signals Synch, Break and the control functions below.
sections.eli5: Imagine everyone agrees to talk through the same plain toy walkie-talkie, even if they own fancier ones at home. Then nobody has to learn how everyone else's gadget works.

sections.title: Data and control functions
sections.content:
Telnet standardises five control functions that most systems already offered but invoked in different ways: Interrupt Process (IP), Abort Output (AO), Are You There (AYT), Erase Character (EC) and Erase Line (EL). They have "standard, but not required, meanings": a system that does not offer a function to its local users may treat the representation as a no-operation, but a system that does must provide the same function to a network user. IP is the exception, because other protocols that use Telnet may require it.

The Go Ahead (GA) command exists for half-duplex terminals with lockable keyboards, such as the IBM 2741. A process that has finished sending data and has no queued input must send GA, so the user's host knows when to hand the keyboard back. The RFC warns that sending it too early can block output.

End-of-line also needs care. The sequence CR LF must be treated as a single "new line", and a bare carriage return must be sent as CR NUL. The RFC says the CR character "must be avoided in other contexts", so a receiver always has a following byte to make a rational decision.
sections.eli5: Telnet has five special buttons: stop that, stop talking, are you there, delete a letter and delete this line. Everybody presses them the same way, so every computer knows what they mean.

sections.title: Commands and the IAC escape
sections.content:
Every Telnet command is at least two bytes: the "Interpret as Command" escape byte IAC (255) followed by the command code. The four option-negotiation commands (WILL, WON'T, DO, DON'T) are three bytes, the third being the option code. These codes only mean something when immediately preceded by an IAC.

Because only IAC needs special treatment, a data byte of 255 is sent by doubling it, IAC IAC, and "the other 255 codes may be passed transparently". That keeps escaping rare, which matters once options let the data stream carry richer content.

The command codes run from SE (240) to IAC (255): NOP (241), Data Mark (242), Break (243), Interrupt Process (244), Abort Output (245), Are You There (246), Erase Character (247), Erase Line (248), Go Ahead (249), SB (250), WILL (251), WON'T (252), DO (253), DON'T (254) and IAC (255).
sections.eli5: A special secret knock tells the other computer, "the next bit is an instruction, not part of the story." If the story itself needs that knock, you knock twice.

sections.title: Option negotiation
sections.content:
Anything beyond the NVT is an option. Either side may ask for one with four words. WILL XXX offers to perform option XXX, and DO XXX asks the other side to perform it. The replies are the positive and negative acknowledgements: DO or DON'T answers a WILL, and WILL or WON'T answers a DO. If a request is refused, the connection simply stays as an NVT. A party "may always refuse a request to enable, and must never refuse a request to disable", and a host that knows nothing about an option can just refuse every request for it.

The syntax is symmetric, which risks endless acknowledgement loops, so there are rules. A party may only request a change of option status, not announce its current mode. A request to enter a mode the party is already in must not be acknowledged, but a request for a change must always be answered. A rejected request should not be repeated until something changes. If both sides request the same option at once, each treats the other's request as the acknowledgement of its own.

If an option needs richer negotiation, such as line length, the options are used to establish that both sides understand it, and then a subnegotiation (SB ... SE) with its own syntax takes over. The companion document is RFC 855.
sections.eli5: One computer asks, "Can we use the fancy mode?" The other says "yes" or "no thanks." You only answer when something changes, or you would both say "okay!" back and forth forever.

sections.title: The Synch signal
sections.content:
A user whose program has run away needs an interrupt that gets through even when data is queued up in the network. The flow control on the Telnet connection may hold such a signal back, so Telnet defines the "Synch": a TCP Urgent notification combined with the Telnet command Data Mark (DM, 242).

The Urgent notification is not subject to the connection's flow control, and it tells the receiver to scan the data stream quickly for "interesting" signals, discarding other data, until it reaches the DM. In normal mode a DM is a no-operation. Several Urgent notifications can be merged, so they cannot be counted. Interesting signals are the standard representations of IP, AO and AYT (but not EC or EL), their local analogues, and all other Telnet commands.

This is also the standard way to flush a data path: a server that receives an AO should return a Synch to the user. By convention the sequence [IP, Synch] serves as an out-of-band signal for other protocols that run over Telnet.
sections.eli5: If a long line of people is blocking the way, you cannot just stand at the back and yell. Synch is like using the emergency door: the message skips past the line and everyone in the line gets told to ignore their chatter until the end marker.

sections.title: Connection establishment
sections.content:
The Telnet TCP connection runs between the user's port U and the server's port L. The server listens on its well-known port L, and since a TCP connection is identified by the pair of ports, it can serve many simultaneous connections on port L from different user ports.

For remote terminal access to service hosts, the RFC assigns server port 23 (27 octal). That is the only port the document specifies.

The RFC says nothing about authentication or encryption. Everything, including login names and passwords typed by a user, crosses the network as ordinary data, which is the main reason Telnet is not used across untrusted networks today.
sections.eli5: The server waits at door number 23. When you knock there, you get a private line to it, and the server can answer many people at once, each on their own line.

cells: Next print line, same horizontal position (required)
Left margin of the current line (required)
Print head one position toward left margin (optional effect)

items.title: Interrupt Process (IP)
items.text: Suspend, interrupt, abort or terminate the process the NVT is connected to. May be required by other protocols using Telnet.

items.title: Abort Output (AO)
items.text: Let the process run on but do not send its output to the user. The server should also send a Synch.

items.title: Are You There (AYT)
items.text: Ask for some visible evidence that the system is still up and running.

items.title: Erase Character (EC) / Erase Line (EL)
items.text: EC deletes the last undeleted character or print position. EL deletes back to, but not including, the last CR LF.

fields.name: IAC
fields.desc: Interpret as Command. Always 255 (decimal), which marks the following byte as a command rather than data.

fields.name: Command
fields.desc: WILL = 251, WON'T = 252, DO = 253 or DON'T = 254. Other commands (NOP 241, IP 244 and so on) are only two bytes long, IAC plus the code.

fields.name: Option code
fields.desc: The option being offered, requested or refused. Option codes are defined in separate option specifications, not in RFC 854.

cells: Data stream part of a Synch; always with TCP Urgent
Start of subnegotiation of the indicated option
Desire to begin, or confirmation of performing, the option
Refusal to perform, or continue performing, the option
Request that the other party perform, or confirmation it is expected to
Demand that the other party stop, or confirmation it no longer is
Data byte 255 when doubled; otherwise the escape

messages.label: IAC DO XXX
messages.note: A asks B to begin performing option XXX.

messages.label: IAC WILL XXX
messages.note: B accepts. The option takes effect immediately.

messages.label: IAC DO YYY
messages.note: A asks for a second option that B does not understand.

messages.label: IAC WON'T YYY
messages.note: B refuses. The connection stays as an NVT for that aspect, and A should not ask again until something changes.

data.title: Sending a STOP string over Telnet out of band
data.code:
1. Send the TELNET IP character:   IAC IP        (255 244)
2. Send the TELNET SYNCH sequence: DM as the only byte,
                                   sent with TCP Urgent
                                   (255 242 in the data stream)
3. Send the character string:      STOP
4. Send the other protocol's analog of the TELNET DM, if any.
